summary: Specifies a certificate extension for including logotypes in public key certificates and attribute certificates. This lets a certificate carry an image such as an organization's logo. It is a proposed standard that has been replaced by RFC 9399.

eli5.summary: A digital ID card can now carry a little picture, like a company logo, to show who it belongs to. RFC 9399 replaced this document.

questions: how to put a logo in a certificate
what is the x509 logotype extension
can a certificate contain a logo
subtitle: How a certificate can carry a pointer to a logo or sound so people can recognize who it belongs to.

tldr.problem: Certificates are built for machines and look technical to people, so users have little help recognizing or choosing between them.
tldr.mechanism: A non-critical certificate extension holds URIs and one-way hashes that point to logotype images and audio. Clients fetch the files, check the hash and show them next to the certificate's identity information.
tldr.outcome: Logotypes are display aids only and never take part in path validation. RFC 3709 has been obsoleted by RFC 9399.

today: RFC 3709 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9399, and it was also updated by RFC 6170. For the current specification, read RFC 9399.

sections.title: Why Put Logos in Certificates
sections.content:
A certificate binds a public key to the identity of a subject. The details that matter to software, such as policies, key usage and name constraints, are not friendly to people. The RFC argues that humans prefer symbols and recognizable marks, and that physical identification instruments such as credit cards and driver's licenses lean on branding for this reason.

The RFC names two problems. Viewing a certificate is often hard to find and too technical, and many applications hide certificates altogether. And when a user must pick one certificate from a portfolio, as when choosing a plastic card from a wallet, logos help tell them apart. Logotypes are the proposed answer. This specification supplements RFC 3280, the Internet profile of X.509.
sections.eli5: Reading a certificate is like reading the tiny print on a card. A logo lets you spot the right card in your wallet at a glance.

sections.title: The Kinds of Logotype
sections.content:
Three standard types are defined. A community logotype is the general mark of a community, such as a card brand that many local issuers co-brand with. An issuer organization logotype represents the organization named in the issuer field. A subject organization logotype represents the organization named in the subject field.

The issuer and subject logotypes MUST be consistent with, and require the presence of, an organization name in the matching name field. Two further types, a loyalty logotype and a certificate background logotype, are carried in otherLogos. The background image MUST let black text be read clearly on top of it, and at most one background logotype is allowed. The RFC says the issuer asserts the link between organization and logo; how an issuer checks it is out of scope.
sections.eli5: There are logos for the group the card belongs to, the company that made the card, and the company that owns it. There are also fun extras like a loyalty badge or a background picture.

sections.title: Logotype Data and Hashes
sections.content:
The certificate does not embed the pictures. It holds a URI for each file and a one-way hash of it, which keeps the certificate small. Two kinds of data exist: image and audio. Implementations MUST support image data; audio is OPTIONAL. Every logotype MUST have at least one image file.

Several files may show the same logotype in different formats or sizes, but they MUST be variants of roughly the same image, and a client MUST NOT show more than one image or play more than one audio sequence for a logotype type at once. At least one image SHOULD be between 60 by 45 and 200 by 150 pixels, and at least one audio file SHOULD play for 1 to 30 seconds. Implementations MUST support JPEG and GIF (image/jpeg, image/gif) and, if they support audio, MP3 (audio/mpeg); animated images SHOULD NOT be used.

CAs MUST include a SHA-1 hash of each referenced file, and clients MUST support SHA-1. A client MUST compute the hash and MUST discard the logotype data if it does not match the extension. All URIs MUST be HTTP or FTP, at least one in each list MUST be HTTP, and clients MUST be able to fetch over HTTP/1.1.
sections.eli5: The card only carries the web address of the picture and a fingerprint of it. If the picture you download does not match the fingerprint, you throw it away.

sections.title: The Logotype Extension
sections.content:
The extension is identified by id-pe-logotype (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1.12), MAY appear in public key and attribute certificates, and MUST NOT be marked critical. At least one of its optional elements MUST be present. The RFC advises avoiding otherLogos where possible.

Logotype data can be addressed directly or indirectly. Direct addressing lists each image and audio file in the certificate itself, which suits a few alternatives. Indirect addressing holds one URI and hash for an external DER-encoded LogotypeData file, which suits many alternatives; that file name SHOULD end in LTD. Clients MUST support both. Issuing applications MUST support direct addressing and SHOULD support indirect addressing. Each image can also carry details such as file size, pixel size, colour or gray scale, and a language tag. Appendix B gives a worked example with one GIF issuer logotype.
sections.eli5: You can write the picture's address right on the card, or point to a list that has many pictures to choose from. A good reader knows how to use both.

sections.title: How Clients Use Logotypes
sections.content:
Logotypes MUST NOT be part of certification path validation or any automated processing. They exist only to improve how a certificate is displayed. If a client cannot support a logotype it MUST NOT report an error and MUST behave as if there were no extension. If the certificate fails validation, the client MUST NOT display any of its logotype data.

A client MAY show none, one or several logotypes, and MAY use any mix of image and sound, subject to local policy. It MUST be able to turn off fetching, and cached logotypes can still be shown. Logotypes appear alongside the identity information and do not replace it. Applications SHOULD cache logotype data.
sections.eli5: The picture is just decoration for people. If your reader cannot show it, nothing breaks, and a card that fails the real check never gets its picture shown.

sections.title: Risks of Logotypes
sections.content:
The RFC admits that logotypes are hard to define and verify securely: it is difficult to say what counts as a legitimate logotype of an organization, and issuers should consider trademark and servicemark implications. A dishonest or careless issuer can put names and logos in a certificate that it has no claim to. For that reason, logos are trusted only if the certificate validates within a valid path.

Two further issues are covered. Fetching logotype data lets a network observer see which clients use certificates with particular logotypes, which is a privacy concern that caching reduces. And a malicious subordinate CA can pass name and policy constraints yet still include inappropriate logotypes. Technical controls do not exist, so the RFC lists contracts, monitoring, certificate policies and revocation as the remedies.
sections.eli5: Anybody could try to print a fake logo on a card. That is why the picture only counts when the card passes the real checks, and why people also rely on rules and contracts.
